citation: Adhvaryu, Achyuta, Prashant Bharadwaj, James Fenske, Anant Nyshadham, and Richard Stanley. 2016. “Dust and Death: Evidence from the West African Harmattan.” Centre for the Study of African Economies, February.
research_question: What is the relationship between dust exposure in utero and infant and child mortality across Western Africa?
data_source: Demographic and health surveys (DHS) from: Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, the Ivory Coast, Liberia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, and Togo.
sample: Data includes: demographic information for mothers, child information incl. length of life, geographic datasets to merge children to the nearest point of dust data.
method: Match child specific information, grouped by survey clusters, to the nearest point of dust data.
explanatory_measure: Satellite data for dust pollution (Aug. 1985 (9 months prior to birth of Apr. 1986 cohort) - Dec. 2006): hourly concentrations of PM2.5.
controls: Child birth order, gender, multiple birth, mother's age at birth, mother's education level, mother's religion.; Rainfall, temperature, country-specific seasonal factors, year-of-birth-fixed effects
key_results: 1) The effect of a one standard deviation increase in in utero PM2.5 exposure leads to a 0.39% increase in infant mortality, roughly 3.5% of the mean (p.17) (I am not sure how many deaths/1000 this correlates to.) 2) The impacts of the dust declined over the years in the study, despite an absence of a reduction in level of dust. 3) Similarly, countries with higher economic development, more mechanized agriculture, more developed healthcare system, and higher rural access to safe water exhibit decreased impacts of PM2.5 on mortality. (See p. 25 for graph of specific macroeconomic moderating factors)
limitations: Uses satellite data to measure PM2.5 levels. Subjects were grouped into clusters, by similar area and matched with the nearest satellite monitoring grid dust point. The maximum distance between each cluster and grid points is not listed and appears to be of significant distance in some locations (p. 14). The spatial resolution of the dust data is more spread out than the DHS. However, PM2.5 can travel great distances so this may not be of concern. Also, authors attempt to account for this in their analysis (p. 27).
related_articles: Jayachandran (2009); Schwartz and Neas (2000)
comments: 1) This is one of the few articles measuring the impacts of PM2.5 in poor developing countries. 2) This study focuses on pollution from naturally occuring dust (made up of "quartz, clay, colloids, and fine mica flakes"), rather than anthropogenic pollution. / One of few articles measuring the impacts of PM2.5 in developing countries.

citation: Ailshire, J. A., and E. M. Crimmins. 2014. “Fine Particulate Matter Air Pollution and Cognitive Function Among Older US Adults.” American Journal of Epidemiology 180 (4): 359–66. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwu155.
research_question: Does PM2.5 exposure increase cognitive decline in older adults?
data_source: Data: 2004 Health and Retirement Study (HRS) survey. HRS collects data about the cognitive status of older Americans as well as other social and demographic pieces of information.
sample_size: Sample size analyzed: 13,996 men and women aged 50 years or older.
method: HRS data was linked, down to the level of the 2000 census tracts, with corresponding PM2.5 air pollution data for that location.
explanatory_measure: U.S. EPA’s Air Quality System national network of air monitoring stations, from 2004.; Pollution data contained 24-hour daily means of PM2.5 from air quality monitors within a 60 km radius of the center of each census tract. Greater weight was given to readings closer to the center of each census tract. Daily means were aggregated to create annual levels.
outcome_measure: Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status:; The test assessed immediate and delayed memory, working memory, processing speed, awareness/orientation, knowledge and language. Test is on a 35-point scale.
controls: Sociodemographic: Age, sex, and race/ethnicity; Socioeconomic: educational attainment, current employment status, household income and wealth. Smoking status was included.; Census tract–level covariates: the proportion of residents aged 25 years or older without a high school degree and median household income
key_results: 1) Living in areas with annual PM2.5 concentrations above EPA standards is harmful to older adults’ cognition. However, there was no linear association identified (i.e. people living in the worst polluted areas were not necessarily the hardest impacted). 2) The results indicated that the strongest identifiable association between increased PM2.5 exposure and cognitive impairment was a decline in episodic memory, which is an early sign of dementia onset in healthy older adults.
limitations: 1) The study could not include air pollution exposure at the individual level (i.e. during commutes and at work), as the only data available was from EPA outdoor pollution monitors within 60km. However, it was noted that given the older demographic, many subjects were already retired and therefore, the influence of workplace and commute air pollution was believed to be minimal. 2) The study utilized data exclusively from 2004 and therefore had limited ability to speak on the impacts of cumulative long-term pollution exposure.
related_articles: Zanobetti and Schwartz (2009); Calderón-Garcidueñas, Reed, and Maronpot (2004); Levesque et al. (2011)
comments: Authors ran secondary analyses which included data that had previously been omitted, for various reasons, and found that their associations still held true.

citation: Anderson, Michael L. 2015. “As the Wind Blows: The Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Air Pollution on Mortality.” Working Paper 21578. National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w21578.
research_question: Estimating the effect of long-term exposure to air pollution, specifically ultrafine particulates (UFP), on elderly mortality rates by using wind patterns near Los Angeles highways.
data_source: Primary metric: Census block, age-specific mortality rate.; This is calculated from 2 data sets which included: info on every death in CA from 1999-2001, associated address, age, and cause of death for each decedent. Also, census block level information such as population by age group, gender, and race.
method: For each census block included, authors calculated: Three-year census block mortality rates for age groups: ≥65, ≥70, and ≥75 years old; distance and direction from the nearest major highway. Authors compared the mortality rates of census blocks that are close together but differ in percentage of time experiencing downwind exposure from highways.
explanatory_measure: Authors tested blocks within the dispersion area of major pollutants: UFP, NO, and NO2. Other pollutants have a shorter dispersion area (p. 4). Each census block located 50-600 meters away from a major highway were studied. Each was assigned a wind speed and direction based off of the nearest weather station data from the previous year.; Notes: 1) 50-600m was determined to be an ideal distance for inclusion given pollutant dispersion distances and avoidance of noisy data near the highway. 2) UFP is <0.1 micrometers in diameter (PM2.5 = <2.5 micrometers in diameter)
controls: Distance from highway (blocks outside of the parameters were excluded) (p. 9), weather station fixed effects
key_results: 1) Authors used different types of regressions: least squares, ordinary least squares (OLS), and two-stage least squares (2SLS). Each produced a slightly different finding:; For least squares, 75+ year old 3-year mortality rate increases by 3% (all causes) with 1 SD increase in downwind frequency. For 2SLS, ceteris paribus, the mortality rate increases by 5%. 2) Overall, moving from the upwind to the downwind side of the highway increases pollution exposure levels by 43% and raises mortality rates by 3.6-6.8% (p. 21). 3) Removing exhaust pollution (i.e. switching to zero-emissions cars) adds an average of 3-months to life expectancy. Given the 1.55 million people in the sample, this would provide an economic gain of $37.2 billion (with VSL=$100,000) (p.23). 4) 70% of the US population lives in urban areas. There are currently no regulations on UFP. There are economic and health benefits to be gained by regulating it.
limitations: Pollution monitors were not used as a part of the main experiment and therefore neither specific pollutants nor their levels are a key part of the findings. On p. 19 they reference limited data from monitors measuring NO2. Also, they note that available monitors did not measure UFP (p. 18)
related_articles: Currie and Neidell (2005); Currie, Neidell, and Schmieder (2009)
comments: 1) Distinguishing the causal effects of air pollution on mortality from unobserved correlated confounding factors can be difficult (p. 3) 2) Details of distances of downwind dispersion plumes of pollutants: UFPM (570-910m), NO and NO2 (550-570m), CO, PM2.5, and PM10 (100-200m) 3) Studies show that without filtration systems, most homes are highly penetrated by UFP. 4) Though there are limited controls used for differing populations, the study relies on comparing nearby, presumably similar, blocks which lie in different directions of wind-blown highway pollution. / Similar elements here to your proposed Nairobi experiment. Includes information about wind direction determination. / Identification: panel, though the authors refer to instrumental variables on p. 14.

citation: Arceo, Eva, Rema Hanna, and Paulina Oliva. 2016. “Does the Effect of Pollution on Infant Mortality Differ Between Developing and Developed Countries? Evidence from Mexico City.” The Economic Journal 126 (591): 257–80. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12273.
research_question: Much of the research regarding the relationship between pollution and infant/neonatal mortality takes place in developed countries. Does this relationship differ between developing and developed countries, given the different social, economic, political, and logistical variances in play?
location: Mexico: many municipalities of Mexico City
data_source: Data: records by municipality (neighborhood) of Mexico City of neonatal (under 28 days) and infant (under 1 year) births and death records; gender; cause of death; municipality of residence.
method: Mortality per 100,000 live births and weekly pollution levels per municipality were calculated. The different data sets were analyzed to identify any correlation. Data from municipalities varying in pollution level was used to estimate the marginal effect of pollution in developing countries as compared to developed countries.
explanatory_measure: Hourly measures of pollution used to calculate maximums for: CO, daily 8-hour average; PM10, daily 24-hour average; SO2 and O3, weekly averages.; Municipalities included in the study were located within 15km of a sensor (in total, 48 out of 56 municipalities in Mexico City).; Note: The description of the pollution measurements used was worded unclearly (p. 9).
controls: Thermal inversion, temperature, weather, time-based fixed effects within each municipality
key_results: 1) A 1% increase in PM10 over a year leads to a 0.42 percent increase in infant mortality. This is comparable to the correlation in the US, despite that PM10 levels in Mexico City are approximately double those in the US. 2) A 1% increase in CO results in a 0.23% increase in infant mortality. This is a larger correlation than in the US. 3) There is a non-linear relationship between CO and infant mortality. There is a linear relationship between PM10 and mortality. 4) Using U.S. data to estimate the benefits derived from cleaner air in the developing world may be biased for pollutants that exhibit a nonlinear relationship between pollution and mortality. 5) The costs of avoidance behaviors differ between developed and developing countries. Therefore, using the relationships between pollution and mortality, estimated in the US, is likely inaccurate for a CBA of environmental regulations. For example avoidance behavior, like health care or cleaner housing, which can play a significant role in pollution-mortality relationships, can be more expensive in the developing world. Thus a relatively small decrease in pollution may have a larger overall health impact in the developing world.
limitations: The pollution data was gathered from what the authors cite as relatively few sensors given the size of the city: PM10, 10 stations from 1997 to 1999, 16 stations after 2000; SO2, 26 stations; CO, 24 stations; O3, 21 stations. They note that these sensors, however, provide accurate data.
related_articles: Currie and Neidell (2005); Knittel, Miller, and Sanders (2011);; Chay and Greenstone (2003); Currie, Neidell, and Schmeider (2009); Zivin and Neidell (2009)
comments: 1) Authors also ran analysis constraining to include only municipalities located within 8km and 10km of a sensor (Appendix Table 2). This increased accuracy of data but decreased the quantity of relevant municipalities. 2) Authors controlled to identify which infant deaths were likely from causes other than pollution (i.e. congenital, accidents, homicides), something that was not mentioned in all similar studies (p. 11). 3) Authors thoroughly compared their findings in Mexico City to findings in comparable studies done in the US, in order to compare the relationship between pollutants in developing and developed countries. See "Related Articles" column for studies utilized. / Highly relevant

citation: Bharadwaj, Prashant, Matthew Gibson, Joshua Graff Zivin, and Christopher Nielson. 2017. “Gray Matters: Fetal Pollution Exposure and Human Capital Formation.” Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 4: 505–42.
research_question: How does CO (and PM10 and O3) fetal exposure affect children's performance on national testing in 4th grade?
time_period: births between 1992-2001 and corresponding test scores between 2002-2010
sample: Sample data: Health: All children born in 1992–2001 in Santiago. Includes: sex, birth weight, length, and weeks of gestation for each birth. Also included demographic information on the parents: age, education, marital status, and municipality of residence. Each mother has an ID number which allowed the authors to implement fixed effects between siblings.; Educational: Test scores for every student, 2002-2010 in the national standardized test which tests math, language, and science.
method: Individuals' health and educational data were matched, providing 623,002 samples. Children's exposure to pollutants while in utero was analyzed as compared to their 4th grade testing scores.
explanatory_measure: Chilean Ministry of the Environment sensor data, 1992-2001 in Santiago. 3 sensors in the city measured: CO, 8-hr moving average; PM10, 24-hour moving average; O3, hourly.; Daily AQI (air quality index) level was calculated using daily pollution level data in order to provide aggregate data.; Children included in the study were matched with the data coming from the closest sensor (no sensor distance constraints).
controls: Weather (incl. temperature), individual level avoidance behavior, season, mother's age and education, student gender
key_results: 1) Strong negative effect from fetal exposure to CO on math and language skills, especially during the 1st and 3rd trimesters (important for brain development).; How much? 1 SD increase in CO exposure during the 3rd trimester correlates to 0.036 SD decrease in math and 0.042 SD decrease in language scores. 2) Between the early-1990's and mid-200's, pollution in Santiago declined by 50+%. Authors estimate that the resulting reduced impact on testing scores could correlate to ~$1,000 per person born during these cleaner years. 3) Poverty also plays a big role in hindering educational attainment. It is difficult to distinguish between the impacts of poverty and pollution on individuals as they often go hand in hand (poor generally live in the most polluted areas).
limitations: 1) Data used likely not as precise as other studies. Authors rely on only 3 pollution sensors for a large city. Many other studies utilize dozens of sensors and constrain analysis for subject distance from sensors. Authors noted that their results were stronger when they ran testing and tried limiting the subject distance from monitors (appendix A3) 2) Study does not control for PM10 as it is highly correlated to CO in terms of origin. Authors note that replacing CO with PM10 yields qualitatively similar results.
theme: Impact on child/infant health and Impact on cognition
related_articles: Articles by Currie and Neidell are highly related
comments: 1) One of the 3 sensors in the study was located at a higher altitude, located above the inversion layers (which trap pollution near the ground). 2) Authors focus heavily on the impacts of exposure during different trimesters of pregnancy. Other studies do touch on this, though not as in depth (see Currie et al. 2009 and Currie and Neidell 2005). / Compares air pollution and mortality rates in the developing world, not just in Western countries.

citation: Calderón-Garcidueñas, Lilian, Antonieta Mora-Tiscareño, Esperanza Ontiveros, Gilberto Gómez-Garza, Gerardo Barragán-Mejía, James Broadway, Susan Chapman, et al. 2008. “Air Pollution, Cognitive Deficits and Brain Abnormalities: A Pilot Study with Children and Dogs.” Brain and Cognition 68 (2): 117–27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bandc.2008.04.008.
research_question: How does pollution exposure impact cognitive functioning and brain structure in children and dogs?
location: Mexico: Mexico City and surrounding area
sample: Test group (from Mexico City, polluted mega city): 55 children from middle class families (age ~10); 7 healthy young dogs; Control group (from low-pollution cities): 18 children from middle class families (age ~10) from Polotitlán, Mex.; samples of brain material from 5 young dogs from Tlaxcala, Mex.
method: Children were given a physical, psychometric testing, gave blood samples underwent a brain MRI (23 children from Mexico City, 13 from Polotitlán). Results for children from both cities were compared and analyzed.; Test dogs had brain MRIs and necropsy (autopsy) conducted (following euthanasia). Control dog brain material was similarly evaluated in a necropsy.
explanatory: PM2.5; PM10; NO2; O3; SO2; CO; Pb
explanatory_measure: Southwest Mexico City:; PM2.5 - annual average concentration of 25 lg/m3; Lipopolyssacharides detected in PM10 samples - 15.3–20.6 ng/mg of PM10; endotoxin concentrations - 59 EU/mg PM10; Polotitlán:; Criteria pollutants: O3, PM10, SO2, NO2, CO and Pb - all pollutant levels are below US standards (as of 2008)
outcome_measure: Psychometric test scores (children), MRI brain scans, blood tests, brain necropsy results (dogs only)
controls: Consistencies amongst sample: All children: come from middle class families, slept in bedrooms with no carpeting/draperies with open windows for ventilation, lived in households with kitchens separated from the living and sleeping areas and used gas for cooking. Mothers' education level was consistent. Risk factors for neurological or cognitive disorders were screened.; Test group dogs: All were mongrels, healthy, vaccinated and raised in indoor-outdoor kennels in Mexico City. Aged 12-19 months.; Control dogs: Raised in Tlaxcala, a city with low pollution 114km east of Mexico City.
key_results: 1) In half of the areas of cognitive testing, children living in highly polluted urban areas exhibited deficits of 2-6% in fluid cognition, memory, and executive functions, as compared to similar children living in the polluted city. 2) 56.5% of the children living in Mexico City city exhibited "white matter hyperintense lesions" on their brains in the MRI. Only 7.6% living in the less polluted city exhibited a single lesion. These lesions are indicative of inflammation and potentially contribute to cognitive dysfunction and other health issues. Dogs from Mexico City, but not from the control city, also had neuroinflammation and vascular lesions. This helps provide further evidence that air pollution is a key factor in cognitive issues (p. 122). 3) Ultrafine particulate matter was observed in the frontal lobe only in the Mexico City dogs. This means that Ultrafine PM can reach the brain and is likely contributing to the neuroinflammation.
limitations: The study has a small sample group. I am not sure if enough children were tested for the results to be definitive. Also, the authors do not track exact pollution levels, though they make a convincing case that pollution is the significant difference between the test and control populations.
comments: A good medical study showing the physical and associated cognitive impacts of PM on the brain.; It is one of the few studies that discuss ultrafine particulate matter. / One of the few medical-focused papers to explore pollution in developing countries

citation: Chang, Tom, Joshua Graff Zivin, Tal Gross, and Matthew Neidell. 2016. “Particulate Pollution and the Productivity of Pear Packers.” American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 8: 141–69.
research_question: How does PM2.5 affect the productivity of indoor physical laborers?
data_source: Data: Payroll records from on Northern CA pear packing factory, 2001-2003. Workers were paid per-crate of pears packed.; Data includes: measures of regular time boxes packed, overtime boxes packed, regular time hours, and overtime hours worked for each packer each day. Daily attendance was also included.
method: Estimate the impact of fine particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) on worker productivity by comparing productivity records with corresponding pollution records for the same time periods.
explanatory_measure: California Air Resources Board monitor, located 2.7 miles from the factory.; Hourly measurements: O3, CO, NO2; Six-day daily average: PM2.5, PM10
controls: Rain, temperature, wind speed, dew point, solar radiation
key_results: 1) A 10 μg/m3 change in PM2.5 decreases productivity by 6%. The impacts of pollution on workers begin at levels well below current US air quality standards. 2) Given that the effects are likely to physiological impairments to a workers' ability to complete physically demanding tasks, other physical laborers are likely to be similarly affected by PM2.5. 3) From 1999-2008, on average, there was a nation-wide decline of 2.79 μg/m3 PM2.5, correlating to a total savings of $19.5 billion dollars. This same decline is estimated to have boosted housing values by $57.3 billion dollars. This is likely an underestimate of the actual value gained because people do not fully measure the health impacts of PM2.5 emissions.
limitations: 1) Despite that the study focuses on PM2.5, their data only includes 6-day averages for PM2.5, meaning that they cannot pinpoint when the workers were exposed to the pollutant, thus making a precise correlation with declining productivity impossible. 2) Authors note, "Given the many uncertainties involved" in this experiment, their calculations are meant to be "illustrative rather than providing a definitive estimate of welfare impacts" of PM2.5 on productivity. The impacts of PM 2.5 are likely much wider reaching than what is calculated in this paper.
related_articles: Zivin and Neidell (2012, 2013, 2014); Bento, Freedman, and Lang (2015)
comments: 1) PM2.5 can penetrate indoors at a rate of 70-100%, other pollutants are far less able to do so. 2) The authors utilized a time period with an uptick of PM2.5 originating from a relatively nearby forest fire to further test their hypothesis. / Presents evidence for fascinating and scary far-reaching implications of PM2.5 emissions.

citation: Chay, Kenneth Y., and Michael Greenstone. 2005. “Does Air Quality Matter? Evidence from the Housing Market.” Journal of Political Economy 113 (2): 376–424.
research_question: How does air quality impact housing prices? What does this say about the priorities and knowledge possessed by home buyers?
data_source: Data: 1) EPA's Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA) yearly county-level attainment/nonattainment designations. 2) Housing values: log median value of owner-occupied housing units in each county. 3) County Characteristics: County-level demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, neighborhood characteristics, fiscal/tax variables, and house characteristics.
method: Compare TSP levels and attainment/nonattainment status with housing prices in order to determine any association reflected in the buyers' marginal willingness to pay (MWTP).
explanatory_measure: Nationwide EPA CAAA monitor network provided monitor-level measures for Total suspended particulates (TSP). Data contained the 4-highest daily readings for counties. Annual county-level geometric mean for TSP was calculated. TSPs include all particulate matter with a diameter <100μm.; TSP, as opposed to other pollutants, was chosen for this study because it has been measured for the longest period by the EPA's CAAA (therefore it has a large dataset) and is known to be detrimental to health.
outcome_measure: Measure of pollution impact: Housing prices
controls: County-level demographic and socioeconomic characteristics (population density, race, education, etc.), neighborhood characteristics (crime rates, doctors, and hospital beds per capita), fiscal/tax variables (per capita taxes, expenditures etc.), and house characteristics.
key_results: 1) Having non-attainment status leads to decreases in pollution in such counties. This corresponds to an increase in housing values at a rate of 0.28% per μg/m^3 reduction of TSP. This is a greater level of MTWP for cleaner air than previously identified. 2) TSP reductions led to a ~$45 billion value increase in the housing market in the mid-1970s across America. 3) From 1974-1980 across the US, TSPs concentrations declined by 6.3 μg/m3 in nonattainment counties and increased by 4.1 μg/m3 in attainment counties. Thus, nonattainment status in that period is associated with ~10 μg/m3 relative improvement in TSPs.
limitations: The study relies on county-level housing pricing data, which is somewhat arbitrary with regards to buyer's tastes (the existence of a county border likely does not alter housing tastes one either side of it, at least with regards to pollution). As such the authors were forced to operate under the assumption that there is a "national housing market" which reflects the MWTP of all Americans. It also means that the authors were not able to accurately examine local trends, like the influence of a coal plant near a specific neighborhood on the local residents' MWTP.
related_articles: Cited by many other papers in this review
comments: Authors note that their meta-analysis of 37 other studies on the same topic predicts that a 1 μg/m^3 decrease in TSP results in a 0.05-0.1% increase in property values. This is less than the findings which come from this paper. They conclude that the "hedonic method" is highly influenced by omitted variable bias. Also, individuals who live in more polluted areas are less likely able to move to cleaner areas due to socioeconomic reasons, and thus have a lower MWTP for clean air. / Very thorough article. Though it doesn't focus on health impacts of pollution, rather people's WTP for housing, given pollution.

citation: Chay, Kenneth Y., and Michael Greenstone. 2003. “The Impact of Air Pollution on Infant Mortality: Evidence from Geographic Variation in Pollution Shocks Induced by a Recession.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 118 (3): 1121–67.
research_question: What effect does a reduction in total suspended particulates (TSPs) have on infant mortality rates? What effect did the 1981-82 US recession, which reduced TSP levels, have on infant mortality?
data_source: Data is derived from the National Mortality Detail Files and National Natality Detail Files.
sample: Infant data: infant births and deaths, weight at birth, cause of death, infant health information, race, gender, county.; Parent data: socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, medical system utilization (incl. prenatal care), maternal health information.
method: Analysis compares changes in infant mortality rates in counties with large TSP reductions with counties with small or zero pollution reduction. Infant deaths are examined at different time periods after birth: 24 hours, 28 days, 1 year.
explanatory_measure: Total suspended particle level (all particles with a diameter less than or equal to 40 micrometers) were measured. Nation-wide data was taken from ~4000 EPA monitors, operating from 1978-1984, which includes data from a period substantial reduction in TSPs during the 1981-82 recession and accompanying decline in industry. The frequency of readings was different at each monitor.; The annual concentration of TSPs for each county was calculated using a weighted average from the data of each monitor in the county, with the number of observations per monitor used as weights.
controls: Weather, cause of infant death, race, gender, twins or more born, parent education information, marital status, immigrant or not, medical system utilization.
key_results: 1) A 1 microgram/m3 reduction in TSPs corresponds to 4.2-6.6 fewer infant deaths per 100,000 live births (with a 0.35 elasticity), for counties with large and medium declines in TSPs in 1981-82. 2) Approximately 2500 fewer infants died between 1980-82 due to the reductions in air pollution. 3) As of 2003, a 1 microgram/m3 reduction in TSPs was associated with approx. 200 additional infants surviving to one year of age. This is worth about $320 million to the US economy (with an assumed VSL of $1.6 million/person). 4) Overall, TSPs have a larger impact on infant mortality than on reduced birth weights. A 1 microgram/m3 reduction in TSPs is associated with a 0.3 gram increase in the average birth weight of infants.
limitations: This study utilizes pollution data on a wide scale: annual monitor-level readings at the county level. While wide-scale trends are important, this study lacks the fine granularity of frequent pollution readings that other comparable studies have. Ex: Simeonova et al. (2018).; Also, the study does not differentiate between PM10, PM 2.5, or other sizes of PM, which are each known to have different health impacts.
related_articles: Cited by: Arceo et al. (2016), Deryugina et al. (2016), Neidell (2004), Zivin and Neidell (2018), Jayachandran (2009)
comments: The author notes that the study is designed to improve on prior studies' flaws. By utilizing the national TSP reduction during 1980-82, a natural event, their study likely circumvents issues of most omitted variable bias (p. 1123). They also may have addressed the issue of the prior TSP exposure influence (in studies of adults) by assigning TSP levels to an infant based off of the mother's exposure during pregnancy and the infant's exposure in the first few months of life. / Most cited across other articles

citation: Currie, Janet, and Matthew Neidell. 2005. “Air Pollution and Infant Health: What Can We Learn from California’s Recent Experience?” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 120 (3): 1003–30. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/120.3.1003.
research_question: Examining the impact of pollution on infant deaths and low birth weights
sample: Population data: Information on all infant deaths 1989-2000.; Variables included: Infant health measures, DOB, mother's age, race, ethnicity, education level, marital status, zip code, prenatal care info, use of public insurance.
explanatory_measure: Measurement: Zip-code level. A weighted average of the weekly pollution level from monitors within a 20-mile radius of mother's zip code.; Data: EPA Air monitoring sensors around California; daily measures of 8-hour maximum for CO and O3; 24 hour average of PM10.
outcome_measure: Health:; Birth weight, infant mortality rate
controls: Weather, the age of the child, race, maternal age, child gender, and other "unobservable characteristics that can be captured by month, year, zip code fixed effects..." (1004).
key_results: Predictors of mortality were consistent with past studies: likelihood of child death increased with being the child of high school dropouts, teenage pregnancies, and people dependent on government insurance, and poor babies were more likely to die. (1021); Postnatal exposure to CO has a high impact on infant mortality. The study found that for every unit of CO reduction per quarter, there was a decline of 11.12 deaths per 100,000 births.; Decreases in CO levels in the 1990s saved ~1000 infant lives in CA. Estimated savings: $1.6-4.8 billion.; The findings for O3 and PM10 were far less significant.
limitations: 1) Maternal smoking was not accounted for because it was not available in the infant health data. Other studies, like Currie et al. (2009), have identified smoking as impactful on infants' health and sensitivity to pollution. 2) Weather data is state-wide while pollution data is zip-code level. This makes it more difficult to measure the true impact of weather on pollution. 3) Avoidance behavior (ex. heeding smog alerts) is not taken into account. Other papers (Neidell 2004) notes that this can impact children's health.
related_articles: Neidell (2004)
comments: During sample period:; -infant mortality rate fell sharply over a short time but trends in low birth weight and fetal death were more stable. This may show that declines in mortality were due to postnatal treatment not improvements in prenatal health.; -There was a significant decline in pollution observed across CA during the time of the survey.; -Because the study attempted to analyze personal levels of exposure but was limited to zip-code sized areas of measurement (rather than personal pollution exposure monitors), the results were more likely to skew towards underestimating the impact of pollutants.

citation: Currie, Janet, and Maya Rossin-Slater. 2013. “Weathering the Storm: Hurricanes and Birth Outcomes.” Journal of Health Economics 32 (3): 487–503. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2013.01.004.
research_question: What effects do severe hurricanes (as a proxy for high stress) have on birth outcomes?
sample: 1) Mother’s demographics: age, race, education, marital status, date of birth, name, residential location. 2) Child data: birth weight and gestational age, sex, birth order 3) Health data: method of delivery, complications of labor and delivery, risk factors for the pregnancy, maternal behaviors i.e. (prenatal care, smoking).
method: Authors compared the birth health outcomes from mothers who lived in the path of the hurricane to those who lived further away, controlling for premature births and other confounders (p. 488).
explanatory_measure: Data on storms and hurricanes: storm/hurricane dates and name, total damages caused in dollars, total number of deaths, location information on the coordinates of the storm path, storm wind speed, and storm type for each day of the storm.
controls: Premature births, mother’s race, age, education, marital status, and number of children, as well as conception year and conception month fixed effects.
key_results: 1) Mothers residing within 30km of the hurricane path during their 3rd trimester are 60% more likely to have a newborn with abnormal conditions and are 30% more likely to have complications during labor and/or delivery. 2)  Hurricane exposure increases the probability that the child required assisted ventilation for over 30 minutes by 1.5% if in the 1st trimester, and 1.3% if in the 3rd trimester (data from table on p. 497). 3)  Hurricane exposure in all three trimesters is associated with an increased probability of Meconium aspiration syndrome, that often has serious long-term consequences for the newborn. The highest rate was a 3.7% likelihood increase if exposed in the 3rd trimester. (data from table on p. 497). 4) Estimates of the effects of hurricanes on babies did not differ significantly by socioeconomic status, race, gender, or birth order.
limitations: None identified. The authors address any limitation I could identify, in the "Robustness" section, on page 498.
comments: This paper spends a larger amount of time than most other studies explaining how they systematically tested the influence of many potentially omitted variables in order to hone in on the direct impact of the hurricane on mothers and birth health outcomes.; The authors clarify: "There are many possible ways for hurricane exposure to affect pregnancy outcomes... we believe we have ruled out some important potential pathways including changes to migration, medical care, and maternal behavior. Therefore, while stress is a “residual explanation” in our context, we believe that our results may reflect the effects of stress itself during pregnancy" (p. 488). / Very thorough

citation: Currie, Janet, and Reed Walker. 2011. “Traffic Congestion and Infant Health: Evidence from E-ZPass.” American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 3 (1): 65–90. https://doi.org/10.1257/app.3.1.65.
research_question: What health impacts did the reduction of automobile emissions associated with the implementation of automatic electronic tolling (E-ZPass) have on infant premature birth and low birth rates nearby? How were nearby housing prices impacted by the implementation of E-ZPass?
data_source: Natality records for all children born in NJ (1994-2003) and PA (1997-2002). Data included: health at birth (weight, gestation time, and more), background information about the mother (race, education, name, birthdate, and marital status), and mother’s address. Only records for babies born to mothers residing near toll plazas were utilized (n=29,677).; Housing prices records: from New Jersey, 1989-2009.
method: Divide mothers into subgroups based off of distance from toll plazas. Compare their premature birth rates and low birth weight incidence from before and after the implementation of E-ZPass in 1999-2000. Compare housing prices at different distances from the toll plazas before and after E-ZPass implementation to identify any short-term impact internalized into the housing market.
explanatory_measure: To gauge level of pollution exposure, mothers were divided into three groups: 1) Those living within 2 km of a toll plaza. 2) Those living within 3 km of a major highway, but between 2 -10 km of a toll plaza. 3) Those who lived 10+ km from a toll plaza.; Note: Those living near highways are presumed to be exposed to increased levels of TSPs, CO, and NO2.
controls: Distance from a busy roadway, birth year, birth month, mother fixed effects, zip code fixed effects, municipality fixed effects (for housing prices only).
key_results: 1) The introduction of E-ZPass reduced premature birth rates by 6.7-9.1% for babies born nearby the toll plazas. This corresponds to averting 255 premature births out of the observed population, at an estimated total benefit of $9.8-13.2 million. 2) The introduction of E-ZPass reduced low birth weight incidence by 8.5-11.3% for babies born nearby the toll plazas. This corresponds to averting 275 premature births out of the observed population. 3) Policies to curb traffic congestion often underestimate the true benefits as they fail to also calculate the health benefits of the associated pollution reduction. The authors estimated that nationwide, reducing infant exposure to traffic congestion could be valued at $444 million per year. 4) No immediate significant impacts were identified on housing prices. This indicates that it may take time for any eventual impacts effects to be felt.
limitations: 1) The study does not utilize pollution monitors to track the actual levels near each toll plaza due to there being only one monitor located near a toll plaza, out of 98 toll plazas included in the study. 2) Also, while the authors' findings are robust, they do not differentiate between plazas that had larger or smaller pollution reductions due to reduced traffic. While the authors' findings appear to be correct, their estimated levels of impact may not be as accurate as if monitors were utilized.
related_articles: Chay and Greenstone (2005)
comments: The author's finding of significant benefit gained from traffic congestion reduction is further strengthened by the finding that housing prices did not immediately respond to the change. This suggests that the estimated birth effect findings were not driven by socio-demographic changes near the toll plazas.

citation: Currie, Janet, Matthew Neidell, and Johannes F. Schmieder. 2009. “Air Pollution and Infant Health: Lessons from New Jersey.” Journal of Health Economics 28 (3): 688–703. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2009.02.001.
research_question: How does pollution impact infant health at birth and infant mortality rates conditional on health at birth?
data_source: Data: Infant births and deaths in New Jersey from 1989-2003 from the New Jersey Department of Health. The birth records used contained detailed information about babies’ health and also about their mothers, including socioeconomic and health details, ethnicity, and address
method: Mothers and babies were matched with the closest sensors and corresponding data matched.
explanatory_measure: From the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection Bureau of Air Monitoring; 8-hour maximums of carbon monoxide (CO) and Ozone (O3); Daily maximums for PM10; Mothers and infants who lived within 10km of a monitor were matched the corresponding pollution data.; Note: Most sensors did not measure all three pollutants.
outcome_measure: Infant birth weight and infant mortality rates conditional on health at birth.
controls: Weather, pollution monitor location.; Mother's: age, education level, marital status, race and smoking habits.; Child's: birth order, if it was a multiple birth, sex.
key_results: 1) Elevated CO exposure has negative effects on infant health both in utero and after birth.; Impacts: reduced birth weight, shortened gestation time, and increase the probability of infant death. 2) A one-unit decrease in CO saves approximately 18 lives per 100,000 births (2.5% reduction in the probability of infant death). In contrast, 1 unit increase in mean CO during the 3rd trimester increases the risk of low birth weight by 8% 3) Infants of smokers are even more susceptible to the negative effects of CO exposure. Infants of smokers were also found to be susceptible to reduced birth weight and shorter gestation time as caused by PM10 and O3 exposure, though the authors noted that they were less confident in these results. 4) Authors compared the data of children born in 1989 and 2003, during which time CO levels across the country declined. The pollution decline is estimated to have averted nearly 450 infant deaths nationwide in 2003, at an estimated annual economic savings of $2.2 billion.
limitations: The authors note that the study’s findings may actually be underestimated. The data utilized was only from live births and it is likely, given the strong detrimental link identified between CO and infant health, that there were stillborn babies, as a result of pollution exposure, who were therefore not included in the data.
related_articles: Currie and Neidell (2005)
comments: The study conducted frequently highlights the fact that its contribution to the literature is its use of location-specific data. Additionally, the study is quite vast, spanning a populous US state over the course of 14 years. Furthermore, the study validates the theory that close proximity of subjects to air monitors (<10km) is critical to accurately gauge the impact of pollution on health.

citation: Currie, Janet, Eric A Hanushek, E Megan Kahn, Matthew Neidell, and Steven G Rivkin. 2009. “Does Pollution Increase School Absences?” The Review of Economics and Statistics 91 (4): 682–94.
research_question: What is the relationship between pollution exposure and school absences (used as a proxy for child health issues)?
data_source: Data: Attendance records, in 6-week attendance periods, from schools in Texas located within 10 miles of pollution monitors, from the largest school districts.; Record also included: data on students’ gender, family income, and ethnicity.
sample_size: n=1,512 schools in the sample, accounting for ~40% of students in public schools, grades 1-8 (totaling over 12 million students).
method: Note: Absences can be used as a proxy for child health that is more sensitive to pollution-impacted diseases than medical records. Often times pollution’s effects are not severe enough for hospitalization but can keep children out of school.; Authors compared the mean absence rates during a given attendance period with the corresponding percentage of days each pollutant (detected by the nearest monitor) exceeds 75% of the EPA threshold.
explanatory_measure: Hourly readings for CO, ozone, and PM10. Only schools located within 10 miles of a monitor were included in the study.
controls: Stable characteristics of schools, years, attendance periods, school-specific variations in particular years, school-specific patterns, systematic variations in particular years and attendance periods, socioeconomic variables, demographic makeup of schools, precipitation, and temperature.
key_results: 1) An additional day with CO levels between 75% and 100% of the EPA Air Quality Standard (AQS) threshold increases absenteeism by 5%. An additional day with a CO level above the AQS increases absenteeism by nearly 9%. (Note: the AQS for CO is 9 ppm) 2) "Only PM10 level between 50% and 75% of the EPA threshold has a statistically significant effect on absences, while higher levels do not, suggesting a possible non-monotonic relationship between PM10 and absences" (p. 691). 3) Authors estimate that absences decreased by 0.8% in 2000-2001 due to reduced levels of pollution in the state. This is significant given that the Texas-wide baseline absence rate was 3.58%.
limitations: The use of school-year attendance records means that the summer pollution levels cannot be used. Ozone is particularly high in the summer due to high temperatures. Authors noted that in Texas, temperatures peak in late-August and September, when children are back in school.
related_articles: Chay and Greenstone (2003); Currie and Neidell (2005)
comments: The authors note that they cannot distinguish between absences due to health effects of pollution and absences caused by avoidance behavior. While this could lead to a problem in interpreting the findings, the authors also note that "to the extent that children miss school in order to avoid pollution, they and their parents still incur a cost, and it is useful to capture this type of avoidance behavior as well as the direct effect of pollution on illness in assessing the total costs of pollution" (p. 684). / This study examines pollution impacts on students that are of an intermediate level of severity. Most other studies either examine severe impacts, hospitalization, or less severe, a decline in test scores.

citation: Currie, Janet, Joshua Graff Zivin, Jamie Mullins, and Matthew Neidell. 2014. “What Do We Know About Short- and Long-Term Effects of Early-Life Exposure to Pollution?” Annual Review of Resource Economics 6 (1): 217–47. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-resource- 100913-012610.
research_question: A literature review of papers examining the question: Does early life exposure to pollution have long-term impacts in life?
method: Each of the 31 papers reviewed utilize "quasi-experimental techniques to develop causal estimates of the effects of early-life pollution."; The content of papers included: Impact of air pollution on infant health (in developed and developing countries), impact on older children, and long-term outcomes (economic and academic).
explanatory_measure: Papers reviewed examined only air pollution because data for it is relatively easy to measure and therefore available.
key_results: General trends/findings from reviewed papers: 1) Many papers attribute health impacts to a specific pollutant(s). However, many pollutants are highly correlated and may come from the same sources. 2) Data that allow for the examination of the link between adult achievement with childhood pollution exposure are rare. Natural experiments utilizing data from before and after large environmental shocks are one way of examining this phenomenon. 3) Avoidance behavior influences the measured impacts of pollution exposure. Even when using an environmental shock as a natural experiment, the passage of time will complicate measurement. 4) Currie et al. develop an econometric model for measuring the compounding impacts of pollution early in life on later-life outcomes (p. 219).
theme: Impact on child/infant and adult health and cognition
comments: The authors posit that the findings of this research lead us to ask:; -Are there threshold levels at which pollutants are safe for the young?; -What factors mitigate the impacts of pollution exposure?; -Can we provide further proof that early-life pollutant exposure impacts both health and long-term economic outcomes? / A lit. review with 31 articles reviewed.

citation: Deryugina, Tatyana, Garth Heutel, Nolan Miller, David Molitor, and Julian Reif. 2016. “The Mortality and Medical Costs of Air Pollution: Evidence from Changes in Wind Direction.” w22796. Cambridge, MA: National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w22796.
research_question: What is the estimated effect of acute PM 2.5 exposure on elderly mortality rate, life-years lost, hospitalizations, and medical costs?
data_source: Daily county-level measures of hospital utilization (inpatient and outpatient) and accompanying costs for elderly individuals. This data is gathered from Medicare records which include 97% of all US elderly (aged 65-100 years). Data includes: illness details, dates of death, age, sex, and county of residence.
method: Use county-level daily fluctuations in PM2.5 exposure to corresponding 3-day mortality rates (deaths/million Medicare beneficiaries). The correlation was used to evaluate the magnitude of impact by PM2.5 exposure on life-years lost (i.e. the value of the years of life lost by those who died & the years of life shaved off of the total lifespan of those who were hospitalized as a result of exposure, but did not die.)
explanatory_measure: Monitors measuring hourly levels of PM2.5, O3, CO, SO2, NO2. (The study focuses primarily on PM2.5); Monitors also measured daily county-level wind direction.
controls: Temperature, precipitation, county-level fixed effects (geographic etc.) variation in pollution transport based off of monitor placement.
key_results: 1) A 1 μg/m3 increase in daily PM 2.5 causes: a significant increase in ER inpatient costs (over $15,000 per million beneficiaries); an increase in total ER visits, including visits that do not result in a hospital admission, by 2.29 per million beneficiaries (p.23). 2) OLS estimates were much lower than for IV, indicating that classical biases were not the only influencing factors (p. 23; findings comparison on p. 42). 3) The nationwide reduction in PM2.5 between 1999-2001 saved ~$15 billion, annually, in mortality costs amongst elderly. 4) Authors measured the life-years lost with increased PM2.5 levels, by incorporating variables such as age, gender, and health history details. With a 1 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5: 11.3 life-years per million people with <1 year of life expectancy are lost. 5) Failure to control for age, gender, and health history when calculating the social burden of life-years lost will cause a tendency to overstate the estimate by a margin of approimately 46%. This is the case in many other studies' estimates.
limitations: Authors note that different counties' pollution monitor readings may not adequately measure the average pollution exposure due to the sparse placement of monitors. This is a challenge for all similar studies not setting up their own monitors. (Note: Authors describe their method of overcoming this on p. 14).
related_articles: Currie and Neidell (2005); Currie et al. (2009); Chay et al. (2003); Chay and Greenstone 2003)
comments: 1) Authors cite many articles utilizing wind direction changes to estimate the impact of pollution (p.5). 2) Contains a good description of PM2.5: characteristics, makeup, origins, regulation, etc. (p. 6). 3) Vast data sets used (97% of US elderly population). 4) Utilized both OLS and IV methods. OLS estimates were consistently lower than IV, indicating that classical biases were not the only biasing factors (p. 23; comparison of OLS and IV on p. 42). 5) This is the first experiment to use high-frequency measurements in order to capture both short-term and delayed (3-day) impacts of pollution. / *Highly relevant paper*

citation: Ebenstein, Avraham, Victor Lavy, and Sefi Roth. 2016. “The Long-Run Economic Consequences of High-Stakes Examinations: Evidence from Transitory Variation in Pollution.” American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 8 (4): 36–65. https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20150213.
research_question: Does PM2.5 exposure decrease performance on standardized tests? How does this impact individual trajectory and earnings, as well as the economy as a whole?
data_source: Data: 1) Israeli national matriculation exam information from 2000-2002. This included: scores, detailed demographic information for each test taker, and exact testing location. 2) Corresponding data on post-secondary education and earnings of the test takers (youngest cohort would have been age 28 at the time of the study)
method: Individual test-taker data and pollution data from the same test days and sensors located within 2.5km of the testing sites were matched. Records of the students' eventual post-secondary education and earnings trajectory are also matched with their test scores and the corresponding air quality levels at their test sites on the testing days.
explanatory_measure: Israeli Ministry of Environmental Protection PM2.5 pollution data, measured at 5-minute intervals and averaged over the duration of each day. These were then converted to Air Quality Index (AQI) units, following U.S. EPA standards. Test taker scores and information were paired with air quality monitoring station data, located up to 2.5km away from testing locations.
outcome_measure: Standardized high school matriculation test scores
controls: Temperature, relative humidity, parental education level, sex.
key_results: 1) Short-term cognitive functioning may be reduced by PM2.5 exposure. An increase of 10 units of PM2.5 (AQI) raises the probability of failure by 2% and lowers matriculation certification rates by 3%. 2) The decreased scores were identified as the beginning of a chain of events leading to decreased national economic efficiency and on the individual level, decreased wages over the lifetime of impacted test takers.
limitations: Solidly laid out study.
related_articles: Neidell (2004)
comments: Authors were vigilant in avoiding misattribution of the impact of pollution. They tested correlation identified between PM2.5 pollution and decreased test scores, by running placebo tests utilizing pollution data from days other than testing days. They found that the placebo pollution dates did not impact the testing scores in the trial, thereby lending further credence to their overall findings.; Another positive indicator of accuracy in the study was that the pollution data gathered was more detailed than in many other comparable studies and the sensors were located only 2.5km away from testing sites. / Contains many similar elements in common with with your proposed study in Nairobi during testing days.

citation: Freire, Carmen, Rosa Ramos, Raquel Puertas, Maria-Jose Lopez-Espinosa, Jordi Julvez, Inmaculada Aguilera, Francisco Cruz, Mariana-Fatima Fernandez, Jordi Sunyer, and Nicolas Olea. 2010. “Association of Traffic-Related Air Pollution with Cognitive Development in Children.” Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health 64 (3): 223–28. https://doi.org/10.1136/jech.2008.084574.
research_question: What is the relationship between NO2 (a surrogate for traffic pollution) exposure and children's motor and cognitive abilities?
sample: Data: male children, age 4 years, were selected from a larger population-based cohort study on prenatal environmental exposures in relation to growth, development and health from early fetal life. Data gathered included child's home location and type (urban, metropolitan, suburban, or rural), child's medical information, parental sociodemographic information.; Each child was tested with the McCarthy Scale of Children’s Abilities (MSCA) standardized test, to evaluate their quantitative, verbal, memory, perceptual performance, and motor abilities.
method: A population-based birth cohort was followed from the age of 4 years for 1 year. Cognitive measures and estimated levels of NO2 exposure were taken in order to evaluate any relation between the two.
explanatory_measure: Home outdoor NO2 levels were estimated as a proxy of individual exposure to traffic-related air pollution.; 26 NO2 monitoring sites were located in the urban area and 50 monitors were located in the centers of the non-urban areas.; Sampling was done in two 7-day periods (Nov. 2005 and Sept. 2006) during the same year as the evaluation of the children. Using a "land-use regression" model, the authors estimated the exposure for urban vs. rural dwelling children and assigned an exposure value accordingly.
outcome_measure: McCarthy Scale of Children’s Abilities (MSCA) standardized test for quantitative, verbal, memory, perceptual performance, and motor abilities.
controls: Sociodemographic covariates: place of residence, maternal and paternal education, maternal occupational status, parity, duration of breastfeeding, type of delivery, marital status, smoking during pregnancy, and age of mothers and children.; Physical covariates: birth weight and length, gestational age.; Psychological covariates: parents’ mental health scale scores and parent-to-infant attachment scale scores.
key_results: 1) Children exposed to higher NO2 levels (>24.75 μg/m3) demonstrated a 4.19 point decrease in their MSCA general cognitive score. Children exposed to lower NO2 levels (15.40-24.75 μg/m3) showed a lower, 1.07 point decrease. This was not found to be statistically significant. 2) In the different subsections of the MSCA, children exposed to >24.75 μg/m3 NO2 had lower scores by: quantitative, 6.71 points; working memory, 7.37; gross motor areas 8.61 points. The identified associations were not statistically significant, except for with gross motor areas.
limitations: The studied area, Granada, Spain has limited industrial activity, and as such, the predicted NO2 likely originates from traffic pollution. While this allows the authors to identify the source of the NO2, it also limits their ability to speak about the impacts of pollution from a diverse array of sources, as is the case in many polluted areas.; Similarly, none of the predicted NO2 concentrations exceeded the European Commission annual mean limit value of 40 μg/m3. This may be a part of the cause of the relatively weak associations identified in the studied.
related_articles: Calderón-Garcidueñas et al. (2008); Suglia et al. (2008)
comments: 1) This paper studies both rural and urban settings for a regional area. 2) This paper studies pollution impacts on children at what are considered to be "safe" levels. This may be a part of the cause of the relatively weak associations identified in the studied. 3) Authors note that "deficits in gross motor skills may... be detectable before other deficits in cognitive function." As such they not that they are in the process of conducting a  psychological follow-up of these children to test this theory (p. 226). / This paper studies both rural and urban settings, something rare amongst regionally focused similar studies.

citation: Grainger, Corbett, Andrew Schreiber, and Wonjun Chang. 2017. “How States Comply with Federal Regulations: Strategic Ambient Pollution Monitoring.” In . UC Santa Barbara.
research_question: How are states perversely incentivized with regards to strategically placing monitors in order to be in compliance with the Clean Air Act and its Amendments (CAAA)? How does this strategic monitor placement impact the pollution levels observed and what downstream impacts does this have?
data_source: Data: Nation-wide Air Quality System (AQS) data from the EPA (~1 million monitors). The data is derived from the ambient air pollution monitors used to determine CAAA compliance across the USA. Monitors measure criteria pollutants and have varying measurement objectives (local or regional pollution levels). Local regulators are charged with the placement of sensors for this national law.; 2 sets of satellite data, from NASA and a "Berkley High Resolution" set, are also used.; Controls: From the American Community Survey, 2006-2010 (see "confounders measured").
method: Satellite data, which is assumed to be unbiased, as placement is not a factor, is used to evaluate whether newly sited ground monitors are strategically placed in order to influence the perceived levels of pollution they are intended to represent. Measurements were conducted using z-scores, where more negative scores indicated pollution avoidance and more positive scores indicated targeting polluted areas.
explanatory_measure: Ground monitor data: Hourly measurements of ozone. The current U.S. National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) level for O3 is 0.075ppm measured using annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentrations averaged over three years (p. 11-12).; Satellite data: High-resolution data set for NO2, Relatively lower resolution dataset for criteria pollutants (p. 13).
controls: At the census tract level: average poverty rate, median age, median rent, population levels, race, percent small children (under age 5), number of point pollution sources present; Economic activity level (at the level of satellite data grid cell).
key_results: 1) New monitors placed in marginal counties, those that are close to the legal limit of pollution, tend to be placed in relatively clean areas. The z-score is -0.231 and is significant at the 0.1% level. 2) New monitors in nonattainment areas (not in compliance with the CAAA limits) are often placed closer to pollution sources to highlight a potential reason for non-compliance (this point was less clear to me). (I could not identify the relevant z-score). 3) Strategic placement of monitors produces inaccurate data which impacts all who rely on it: econometric studies, socioeconomically disenfranchised populations who would benefit from CAAA protection.
limitations: Satellite pollution data and ground data are measured in mismatched units which require outside information in order to compare. In the text, the authors describe their workaround solution to this issue: "The satellite data are measured as column densities (molecules/cm2), while ground level pollution is monitored in either parts per billion (ppb) for NO2 or parts per million (ppm) for ozone. Converting the column densities to ground level estimates would require the use of an atmospheric model which considers things like average meteorology, topography, etc." As such, we just use the raw column densities as our pollution estimates which is not problematic if considering within-zone variation of the data points around each sensor, as opposed to variation across sensors. We circumvent the issue with the introduction of localized z-scores" (p. 15).
related_articles: Muller and Ruud (2018)
comments: The overall findings of strategically placed monitors raise significant questions about the accuracy of available data for research. Presuming that the pollution data is skewed such that polluted areas are not properly identified, many of the econometric studies conducted in the US with this data could be subsequently inaccurate. The real world implication is that the populations living in polluted areas, which are being made to appear to be less dirty, will be the ones to bear the burden by losing out on forced pollution reduction. / This article is one of only two dealing with monitor placement decisions.

citation: Greenstone, Michael, and Rema Hanna. 2014. “Environmental Regulations, Air and Water Pollution, and Infant Mortality in India.” American Economic Review 104 (10): 3038–72. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.104.10.3038.
research_question: How did Indian government policies impact water and air quality? How did these changes in turn affect infant mortality rates?
data_source: Data: Annual city-level infant mortality data. City-level sociodemographic characteristics, corruption, social activism data. District-level population, literacy rates, expenditure per capita. State-level demand for clean air and water and the degree of local corruption and institutional quality, each year (gathered from quantity of Times of India newspaper mentions of the topic).
method: Compare air and water pollution data, and infant mortality rates, with the timing implementation of policies intended to reduce pollution. Authors sought to identify if the policies led to a reduction in infant mortality rate due to reduced pollution levels. The authors also utilized mentions about cleaner air and water in the Times of India newspaper in order to identify the influence of public demand for cleaner air and water on success of related policies.
explanatory_measure: Air Pollution: Measures of NO2, SO2, and PM (diameter <100μm), by 572 monitors in 140 cities across the country, from 1987-2007. Dataset does not include all cities and all monitors each year. The frequency of readings was not listed.; Water Pollution: Quarterly of monthly river data observations from 489 monitors in 424 cities (along 162 rivers), 1986-2005. Measures: biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), an indicator of water quality; dissolved oxygen (DO), another indicator of water quality; and fecal coliforms (FColi), a count of coliform bacteria per 100ml of water.
controls: City fixed effects, year fixed effects, per-capita consumption and literacy rates.
key_results: 1) Implementation of a catalytic converter requirement was strongly associated with air pollution reductions. In the 5 years following the policy's enactment (1996-2000), pollution levels decreased by the following amounts: PM by 48.6 μg/m3, SO2 by 13.5 μg/m3, and NO2 4.4 μg/m3. The PM and SO2 declines are statistically significant. The NO2 decline was not. These declines are 19 percent, 69 percent, and 17 percent of the 1987–1990 nationwide mean concentrations, respectively (p. 3058). 2) For the Supreme Court Action Plan (SCAP) air pollution policies, there is scant evidence of a change in PM or SO2 concentrations, and only minor evidence for an impact on NO2, when controlling for pre-existing trends. 3) There is little evidence suggesting that The National River Conservation Plan (NRCP), which began in 1985, reduced water pollution. BOD and DO have worsened and FColi levels have not changed significantly. 4) The catalytic converter policy is associated with a reduction in infant mortality rate of 0.64 per 1000 live births. However, the authors feel that this estimate is imprecise and not statistically significant. 5) The success of pollution policies in developing countries with weak governmental institutions is dependent on popular support and the support of stronger institutions. This is the reasons for the relative success of air quality protections in India.
limitations: 1) In India, many births and deaths are not registered with the government. This is likely a greater problem with unreported deaths and thus the true infant mortality rate is likely higher than indicated by the data. As such the authors' findings likely underestimate the impact of pollutants on infant mortality. 2) When authors derived their levels of demand for clean air and water from newspaper mentions, it is possible that these mentions do not correlate with public demand. Authors posit that, "it is possible that the greater mentions reflect differences in water or air pollution concentrations or some other factor" instead (p. 3065).
comments: Authors state that their dataset gathered and used is the most comprehensive city-level panel dataset amassed for air and water pollution as well as environmental policies for any developing country, to date. / Fascinating paper. However, much of the research in this paper is evaluating why certain government policies worked to lower pollution, or not. The focus on infant mortality is a relatively small part of the study.

citation: Gupta, Pawan, Sundar A. Christopher, Jun Wang, Robert Gehrig, Yc Lee, and Naresh Kumar. 2006. “Satellite Remote Sensing of Particulate Matter and Air Quality Assessment over Global Cities.” Atmospheric Environment 40 (30): 5880–92. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosenv.2006.03.016.
research_question: Prior studies have shown a relationship between satellite-derived aerosol optical thickness (AOT) data and PM air quality on earth. This paper adds to the literature by expanding on this evidence for urban areas outside of the US in order to test the reliability of this relationship for predicting ground-level PM2.5.
location: Satellite data for:; New Delhi, India, Australia, Hong Kong, Switzerland, &; New York, USA
data_source: 1 year of data (2002).; The MODerate resolution Imaging Spectro-radiometer (MODIS) aerosol optical thickness (AOT) and PM2.5 mass were collocated in space and time for inter-comparative and quantitative analysis
explanatory_measure: MODIS data measuring AOT across a certain geographic area, called a pixel, was matched with PM2.5 measurement station data located within 25km of the pixel. PM2.5 hourly measurements were averaged daily.
controls: Ambient relative humidity, wind speed, cloud cover, and height of the mixing layer.
key_results: Ground sensors are accurate measures of point PM2.5 pollution but are not an efficient/effective means of mapping regional to global distribution of aerosols. Satellite-derived data could fill this gap, especially in developing countries with limited measurement capabilities.; Satellite data can also better track the origins of PM and its spread around regions and the world.; Findings for air quality condition during the study period: Sydney and Switzerland - good; NYC - moderate; Delhi and Hong Kong - not good.
limitations: Limitations of satellite data use:; Relevant only for relatively large spatial areas, not specific neighborhoods; Measures ambient conditions that can be influenced by weather, while PM2.5 ground-level monitors measure surface-level dry particle concentrations.
related_articles: Zhang et al. (2005)
comments: Much of the paper contains highly technical details of the process of satellite data gathering and interpretation.; In this paper, 'aerosols' refer to particles suspended in the air/ atmosphere; A visual explanation of the satellite measurements techniques can be found: https://arset.gsfc.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/airquality/workshops/BAQ16/P8.pdf

citation: Jayachandran, S. (2009). Air quality and early-life mortality: Evidence from Indonesia’s wildfires. Journal of Human Resources, 44(4):916–954.
research_question: What impact did Indonesia's 1997 forest fires have on fetal, infant, and child mortality before age 3?
data_source: Early-life mortality statistics: Given the lack of direct mortality records available, the author was forced to estimate "early-life mortality" numbers, or death before age 3, using the 2000 Indonesian population census data. They calculated the number of inferred "missing children" (infants and children who died, as a result of pollution exposure in utero or early in life) by comparing post forest fires population numbers with those from before the fire (p. 921).; Food consumption data (socioeconomic): National Socioeconomic Survey, an annual household survey.; Healthcare data: 1996 "Village Potential Statistics", a census of community characteristics including available healthcare, and cooking fuel used in homes.; Fire data: Satellite monitoring of the extent of the wildfires.
method: The author utilizes satellite data of exposure to smoke pollution (particulate matter and other types) caused by the forest fires to estimate its impact on early-life mortality for a cohort of children born just before and after the fires.
explanatory_measure: Satellite ozone monitoring: "Daily aerosol measures" (constructed from observations from over 3 days) from points located ~175km apart. Author calculated daily ozone measures for studied subdistricts taking ozone observation points located within 100km of the center of each subdistrict and weighting them according to each's distance from the subdistrict center.; In total, 226 unique ozone pollution grid points were used to measure 3700 subdistricts.
controls: Precipitation, fire intensity, mother's education, urban or rural location, month fixed effects, subdistrict fixed effects.
key_results: 1) During the 1997 fires, in hard-hit areas, PM10 pollution levels reached 1000 mg/m3 on several days, and exceeded 150 mg/m3 for long periods. The EPA PM10 standard is 150 mg/m3 as a 24-hour average, to be exceeded only once annually. 2) The 1997 wildfires led to an estimated 15,600 early-life deaths, or a 1.2% decline in birth population. 3) Pre-natal exposure to pollution had a smaller effect on mortality rates in higher income areas, though the experiment cannot decisively explain why. After controlling for many variables, some explanatory theories are that poorer people; have less access to medical care, have worse health, cook with wood-fired stoves and are were thus doubly exposed to smoke pollution.
limitations: Author's use of inferred levels for "missing children" is both unique and also leaves the potential for misestimation. Though the author believes that she successfully controlled for potentially confounding variables, there is still room for error. With that said, it is possible that her early-life mortality estimation would still be more accurate than official records, if they were to exist, given the limitations of accurate record-keeping in developing countries.
related_articles: Chay and Greenstone (2003); Currie and Neidell (2005)
comments: Author's use of census data to infer "missing children" is creative and one I have not seen in other studies. There is potential for error in the author's estimation (p. 922-923), though she addresses each and believes that they did not influence her findings.; The author also utilizes multiple proxies for variables that were difficult or not feasible to measure. For example, food consumption as a proxy for income level (p. 939). / This is one of the few natural experiments. Unique methodology too.

citation: Morales, Eva, Jordi Julvez, Maties Torrent, Rafael de Cid, Mònica Guxens, Mariona Bustamante, Nino Künzli, and Jordi Sunyer. 2009. “Association of Early-Life Exposure to Household Gas Appliances and Indoor Nitrogen Dioxide With Cognition and Attention Behavior in Preschoolers.” American Journal of Epidemiology 169 (11): 1327–36. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwp067.
research_question: What is the effect of early-life exposure to household gas appliances and indoor nitrogen dioxide on cognitive functioning and inattention and hyperactivity symptoms in preschoolers?
sample: Data: children, information on their neurodevelopmental assessment, gas appliances at home, and indoor NO2 concentrations for the first 3 months of the child's life. Also, DNA samples were taken to identify a child's genetic type of "glutathione S-transferase P1" gene (GSTP1). Certain types of GSTP1 are involved in antioxidant defenses to protect against oxidative stress. NO2 is an oxidative stressor and thus the authors theorized that the possession of protectant GSTP1 could reduce the impacts of NO2 exposure on applicable children.
method: Multivariate linear regression models were used to examine the association between gas appliances or indoor NO2 concentration and cognitive and behavioral outcomes at age 4 years.
explanatory_measure: Measures collected in each family's home during the first 3 months of the child's life: dust samples, average 2-week indoor NO2 concentrations, a questionnaire on household characteristics (cooking appliances, heating, and cooling systems, number of hours of ventilation, and size of the house).
outcome_measure: cognitive functioning score and observed attention/hyperactivity behaviors
controls: Maternal and paternal: years of education, social class, tobacco smoking habits.; Maternal: marital status, medical history, parity, dietary intake during pregnancy, alcohol consumption during pregnancy, type and duration of breastfeeding.; Child: Anthropometric measures at birth, gestational age, child’s sex.
key_results: 1) Children with exposure to gas appliances in their homes were at higher risk of inattention, but not hyperactivity. 2) "Adverse effects of exposure... were found in children with any GSTP1 Val-105 allele but not in children with the Ile/Ile genotype" (p. 1331). "Exposure to gas appliances was associated with a decrease of 9.72... points in the general cognitive score and with an increased risk of inattention for children with any GSTP1 Val-105 allele" (p. 1332). 3) "Children with the less active GSTP1 Val-105 variant, brain cells are more susceptible to biochemical changes induced by early-life exposure to nitrogen dioxide" (p. 1333).
limitations: 1) Compared to nonparticipants, participants had higher general cognitive scores and were of a higher social class. Therefore, it is possible that the results could be skewed. If so, I would assume that the results would underestimate the impacts of indoor pollution as higher class families generally have better access to medical care and nutrition, reducing negative impacts of pollution exposure. 2) The study sample size is quite small and thus its findings may not be generally representative.
comments: This is a unique study in that it is evaluating the health risks associated with pollution from technology that is presumed to be the cleaner option, as compared to wood-burning stoves and heating. As such, gas appliances are more common in the developed world. / This is a unique study in that it focuses on the impacts of gas appliances, which are considered to be "clean".

citation: Muindi, Kanyiva. 2017. “Air Pollution in Nairobi Slums Sources, Levels and Lay Perceptions.” Umeå: Umeå University.
research_question: To assess indoor sources and levels of air pollution in slum households and gather data about perceptions of the risks of air pollution.
location: Two slum communities, Korogocho and Viwandani, near Nairobi, Kenya
data_source: Quantitative study: Data from a Nairobi health and demographic longitudinal survey, and others, included socio-demographic information on all residents, migration information, household wealth, pregnancies, births, and deaths.; Focus Groups: Focus groups were convened to learn about individual and community views regarding indoor and outdoor air pollution. Topics included perceptions of sources of air pollution, views and attitudes on individual and government responsibility for addressing air quality issues, and discussion of health impacts of air pollution.
method: Group data was collected in focus group discussions (FGDs).
